newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria to privatise more than 250 firms soon.
newsitem.headline: Algeria to privatise more than 250 firms soon.

text.p: Algeria, trying to speed up its slow privatisation process, will offer more than 250 state-owned firms and industrial units for sale to private investors soon, an official at the industry ministry said on Saturday.

"The detailed list of over 200 companies and more than 50 units in the industrial sector will be published shortly after the adoption of new privatisation legislation," the official told Reuters by telephone from Algiers.

The government-appointed Transitional National Council, a quasi-parliament, will hold a voting session on Sunday on a new privatisation law changing Algeria's previous cautious approach to sell off state-owned firms.
Privatisation, adopted as a major policy some 18 months ago, is a thorny issue in Algeria.

Many local and foreign economists are urging the rapid sale of state-owned companies in a drive to modernise them while officials fear a mass sell-offs might bring more upheaval to the delicate balance of civil strife locking the government in conflict with Moslem guerrillas, a market analyst said.

The country has been gripped by violence for the past five years during which about 60,000 people have died. Officials have said that poverty and lack of jobs and houses drove many young people into the ranks of armed Moslem fundamentalists trying to turn the North African country into a strict Islamic state.
Algeria has a complex privatisation rules allowing for share transfers, management buyouts and complete sale to outside investors.
Algerian officials said the slow privatisation in the past 18 months was only a test and bold privatisation was expected to begin this year.

Weak local savings and relatively tough conditions for sell-offs underpinned in the previous privatisation law did little to foster the privatisation process, with only 10 businesses among more than 70 offered for sale found investors.
About 130,000 workers are likely to lose jobs in 1997 and 1998 as the government plans to shut down about 60 units, roughly half of them in the industrial sector, the official said.

More than 70,000 among the redundant workers will benefit from a social scheme set up by the government to cushion reform impact on the poor while the 60,000 others will either change jobs or get early retirment.
